Visual artist Jason Cook  creates kinetic sculptures and robotic installations using electronics, programming and mechanical engineering. In The Walking Chair (2025), an ordinary wooden chair is transformed into a moving machine. A system of motors, mechanical parts and electronic components is attached beneath the seat, allowing the chair’s legs to move. By giving a familiar piece of furniture the ability to walk, Cook changes the way we perceive an everyday object. The chair is no longer simply something we sit on  it becomes an object with a movement of its own. #art #artist #weird #chair #avantgarde

En este video, un robot masilla las juntas de los paneles de yeso, demostrando precisión y eficiencia en cada movimiento, sea real o animado, nos invita a reflexionar:  En el futuro, los robots realizarán muchos de los trabajos difíciles, repetitivos y peligrosos que hoy enfrentamos. Pero hay algo que las máquinas no pueden replicar: nuestra creatividad, nuestra ética y nuestra capacidad de soñar.Los robots serán nuestros aliados, facilitando nuestras labores y permitiéndonos enfocarnos en lo que realmente importa. Seremos nosotros quienes diseñemos, innovemos y tomemos decisiones basadas en valores humanos.Mientras los robots se encargan del trabajo arduo, nosotros, los humanos, seguiremos liderando con imaginación y corazón. iRobot co-founder Colin Angle, whose company sold over 50 million Roombas, has unveiled his new venture, Familiar Machines & Magic. Its first product is a furry, bear-like quadruped robot with 23 motorized joints, a touch-sensitive coat, cameras, and microphones. The robot communicates through expressive movements rather than speech. A custom onboard AI gives it personality and memory while keeping user data off the cloud. Beyond companionship, it aims to reinforce healthy routines, like limiting screen time. Angle compares its cost to pet ownership, targeting sales next year. Whether it can sustain long-term engagement, where past social robots failed, remains the big question.

videos.caption: I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

In 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen rolled a cabinet into the court of Empress Maria Theresa in Vienna. On top sat a life-size wooden figure in a turban and robe. People called it "the Turk." Kempelen opened the doors one at a time to show the gears, then the Turk played chess and beat almost everyone. It toured Europe for decades. Benjamin Franklin played it in Paris and lost. In 1809 Napoleon played it at Schönbrunn. He made illegal moves. The Turk put the piece back each time, and on the third cheat it swept every piece off the board. The secret was a human chess master hidden inside. He slid on a seat from one side to the other as each door was opened. A candle lit his little board, and its smoke escaped through the Turk's turban. #history #weirdhistory #chess #napoleon #benjaminfranklin #robot #automation #animation #funnyhistory
